description: Team Eclairs is building a crop-rotation decision tool for the Field Shift challenge. I am a data engineer working with real-time sensor data, so I’ll handle pipelines for NASA Earth observations (soil moisture, rainfall, temperature) and local soil data. We’re looking for a frontend/UX developer, someone with ML or data science skills, and anyone who knows agronomy or farming. Curious beginners are welcome too. Let us help farms adapt!
summary:
CropOrbit is a smart crop rotation planner that helps Norwegian farmers decide what to plant, understand why, and estimate what they could earn.

The application maps farms across Norway and shows their crop history from 2017 to 2026, using open data from the Norwegian Agriculture Directorate. To recommend next season's crops, it predicts yields with a model built on NASA Earth observations: Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 vegetation (NDVI) and bare-soil (BSI) indices, and NASA POWER temperature data, trained on official county yields. Predicted yields are turned into gross margins using fertilisation norms and World Bank fertiliser prices, and rotation rules filter out choices that would harm the field.

Farmers get their top three crops with a yield range and a reason, and can use a profit simulator to compare poor, typical and good seasons with their own grain and fertiliser prices. The public map also lets them see what nearby farms grow.

CropOrbit connects historical farming data, environmental conditions and economic scenarios in one accessible tool, helping farmers make better rotation decisions as growing conditions change.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

CropOrbit helps Norwegian farmers decide what to plant next season. A farmer finds their farm by name or organisation number, or clicks any spot on the map, and gets the three crops with the highest expected gross margin for 2027 that still follow sound rotation rules. Each recommendation shows a yield range, the margin in NOK per decare, and a one-line reason based on what the satellite data shows about that field. A profit simulator lets farmers test poor, typical and good seasons with their own grain and fertiliser prices and area.

CropOrbit also maps what 54,066 Norwegian farms (99.6% of all farms in the records) have grown each year from 2017 to 2026. Users can select up to three crops, scrub through the years, and open any farm's year-by-year rotation history and property boundary.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Crop history:
We clean and join Landbruksdirektoratet's open production subsidy data (crop areas for 27 crop codes per farm and year), geocode farms through the farm-centre register and Kartverket's Eiendom API, and map old municipality numbers from the 2018, 2020 and 2024 reforms to current ones using SSB KLASS.

2. Yield model:

for sample grain farms in every county (2017–2024), we extract NASA Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS v2.0) summer NDVI and spring Bare Soil Index, and hot days above 25 °C from NASA POWER. A ridge "anomaly" model per crop predicts yield as the county's normal yield (from SSB table 04610) plus the effect of how this field's NASA features differ from its county. The yield range is the county's real season-to-season spread (10th–90th percentile, including the 2018 drought).

3. Validation:
With leave-one-year-out cross-validation, the model has lower error than the county-average baseline for every crop: spring wheat 18%, oats 13%, barley 9%, rye and triticale 8%.

4. Economics:

Gross margin = predicted yield × price − fertiliser cost − other costs, using NIBIO fertilisation norms and World Bank Pink Sheet fertiliser prices, with optional Felleskjøpet grain prices and Yara fertiliser prices. All values are editable in a configuration file.

5. Rotation rules:
no third year of the same cereal, no winter crop after a late harvest, and only crops grown in that county.

6. Field health:
in each farm panel, Copernicus Sentinel-2 NDVI and BSI time series (5-day composites, cloud and snow masked) show how the current season compares with previous ones.

NASA DATA USED

- Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLSS30 and HLSL30 v2.0), accessed through NASA CMR with earthaccess: NDVI and BSI, the core features of the yield model.

- NASA POWER daily agroclimatology: temperature, hot days, growing degree days, precipitation and FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Existing Norwegian farm software focuses on this season's fertiliser plan. CropOrbit adds the question that comes before it: what should this field grow next year, and why? Farmers get an evidence-based, explainable recommendation in three clicks; advisors get one consistent view of crops, rotations and margins across the country. Better rotations protect soil health, reduce bare-soil periods and erosion risk, and help farms keep their income stable as growing conditions change. Because HLS and POWER are global, the same approach can be retrained anywhere with regional yield statistics.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- The anomaly model combines official county yield statistics with field-level NASA observations, so it works even though Norway has no open field-level yield data.

- Every recommendation explains itself, naming the NASA feature that drove it.

- It turns a decade of Norway's open subsidy records into an explorable national map of crop rotations.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python (pandas) for the data pipeline and model training; FastAPI for the API; React 18, TypeScript and Vite with MapLibre GL for the web app; nginx and Docker Compose for deployment. Data APIs: NASA earthaccess/CMR, NASA POWER, Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (Sentinel Hub Statistical and Process APIs), SSB PxWeb and KLASS, Kartverket Eiendom API, and the World Bank commodity price data. Basemaps from Kartverket and Esri.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty about uncertainty: yields are shown as ranges, and we report which features did not help. Growing degree days, precipitation and water balance were computed but did not add skill with eight seasons of data, so they are not used in the model.

- Data limits: subsidy data is reported per farm, not per field. Demo farms get field-level NASA HLS features, while other farms are clearly labelled "Regional estimate". NDVI is currently averaged over the whole property, which can include forest; clipping to farmland is the next step.

- Transparency: price and norm values are editable, and the app shows a "Placeholder prices" badge until real values are set.

- Usability and access: colour-blind-safe colours, light and dark themes, keyboard navigation, mobile layouts and shareable links.

- Reliability and cost: data that changes yearly is precomputed into a static layer, all downloads are cached so the demo works offline, and every data source's licence and attribution is documented.

NEXT STEPS

Clip satellite indices to farmland (NIBIO AR5), add field-level geometry, add GPM IMERG precipitation and SMAP soil moisture, and include phosphorus and environmental runoff in the recommendations.
